sections.html:
Saline County, southwest of Little Rock, grew from 123,416 residents in 2020 to an estimated 133,288 in 2025. Benton, the county seat and largest city, went from 35,014 to 38,898 over the same stretch, and Bryant from 20,663 to 22,815, an increase of 10.4 percent. Both are commuter suburbs of the capital, connected by Interstates 30 and 530.

Other places in the county include Bauxite, Alexander, Avilla, East End, Haskell, Salem, Shannon Hills, Traskwood and part of Hot Springs Village. One assessor and one collector serve them all, so the same county calendar applies no matter which town you live in. Hot Springs Village also has a private property owners' association, which adds a second set of rules and dues for sellers there.

Benton, Bryant, Bauxite and Harmony Grove school districts each serve part of the county. The Benton School District covers most of Benton, Bryant Public Schools runs Bryant High School, and the Harmony Grove district serves a small area near Frontage Road. The same street can fall in different districts, and some buyers pick the district before they pick the house, so confirm yours before you list.

The assessor, the county clerk and the collector share the work. The assessor's office is at 215 N. Main, Suite 7 in Benton, phone 501-303-5623. The collector is at 215 N. Main St., Suite 3, phone 501-303-5620, email info@salinecollector.org.

Taxes are collected from March 1 through October 15 of the year after they are assessed, in person, by mail or online. In person, the office takes cash, checks, cashier's checks, money orders, debit and major credit cards. By mail, personal checks are accepted only for current taxes.

Notices that went out in July are not tax bills, and the higher values will not appear on the October 2026 payment. Arkansas requires a countywide reappraisal every four years, and increased values take effect the following year. Only owners whose value rose get a notice, so a property that fell in value gets no letter. Some residents were confused, and some received a notice for the first time.

  • Call the Saline County Assessor's Office first if the value looks wrong.
  • If you still disagree, appeal to the Saline County Equalization Board.
  • Requests are filed with the county clerk, and the state deadline is the third Monday in August.

A buyer's taxable value in Saline County can step up by as much as 5 percent a year on a homestead and 10 percent on other real property, until it reaches full assessed value. New construction, newly discovered property and substantial improvements fall outside those caps.

The homestead credit is up to $500 a year, rising to $600 for 2026 bills. A seller 65 or older, or disabled, who receives the credit can hold the assessed value steady, but the freeze does not move to the buyer. The buyer applies on their own after purchase.

sections.h2: How to appeal a new value
sections.html:
A notice showing a higher value is the moment to check your record. Look at the square footage, the number of bedrooms and baths, outbuildings that no longer exist and the condition rating. If anything is wrong, the assessor's office at 501-303-5623 can often correct it with a phone call and a short visit.

When the details are right but the value still seems high, collect evidence before you file. Sales of similar houses in your neighborhood, photographs of damage and repair bids all help. The Equalization Board hears requests that are filed through the county clerk, and the third Monday in August is the last day to schedule.

Because only owners with an increase get a notice, a neighbor who received nothing is not evidence of a mistake. It usually means that neighbor's value stayed flat or went down.

sections.h2: Paperwork to gather before you list
sections.html:
A tidy folder shortens every step. Pull the last tax statement and proof of payment, the deed, any survey and the permits for roof or drainage work. If you rent the house, find the lease and the tenant's contact details. If the house is in Hot Springs Village, request the property owners' association statement as well.

Heirs should collect the documents that show who owns the house now. The title company will ask for them before it schedules a closing, and every missing page adds days.

Benton has a humid subtropical climate, with about 53.41 inches of precipitation a year. A buyer's inspector will look hard at drainage, gutters and the roof. Houses with deferred repairs after wet seasons often struggle in a retail listing, and a cash buyer prices the work in instead of asking you to finish it first.

Plan around the October 15 close of the collection season. Anything unpaid after that date picks up a 10 percent penalty under state law. If you are closing close to the deadline, ask the title company who will pay and whether the payment is made before or after the closing date, then keep the receipt for your own file.

Since the office accepts cards, checks and cash in person, a payoff at closing can usually be handled the same day. Mailed personal checks work only for current taxes, so use a certified or cashier's check when paying back taxes by mail.

If the property has delinquent tax, call the Collector at 501-303-5620 for a payoff amount. The balance is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company records the new deed.

Plan for the buyer's side as well. Saline County bills a year behind, so the closing statement shows how the tax is split. If the reappraisal notice raised your value, the new figure affects the buyer's first full bill, not yours.

sections.h2: What Saline County sellers usually face
sections.html:
• Heirs of a Benton or Bryant house who live elsewhere and want to settle it before the next tax season.
  • Owners of rental houses with a reappraisal notice and a tenant on a lease.
  • Sellers at Hot Springs Village who deal with the property owners' association along with county offices.
  • Houses with deferred roof or drainage repairs after wet seasons.

A direct purchase fits when repairs and showings are the obstacle. Compare any offer with your payoff and the Collector's figure to see what you would net.

Once an offer is accepted, a title company searches the record for unpaid taxes, liens and recorded problems. Have the last tax statement, the deed and any notices from the assessor on hand. The Collector's phone number is the fastest way to get a payoff.

At closing you sign the deed and the title company pays the balance from your proceeds and files the deed with the county clerk. A cash sale with a clean search can close on a date you choose, since there is no lender or appraisal to wait for.

faqs.q: Who is the Saline County tax collector?
faqs.a: The Collector's office is at 215 N. Main St., Suite 3 in Benton, phone 501-303-5620.

faqs.q: When will 2026 reappraisal values show up on a Saline County tax bill?
faqs.a: They take effect next year, not on the October 2026 payment.

faqs.q: Do I get a notice if my Saline County value goes down?
faqs.a: No. Notices are sent only when a property's value rises.

faqs.q: How often does Saline County reappraise?
faqs.a: Every four years. The current cycle ends in 2026, with Trimark Appraisals working across 78,135 parcels.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Saline County house that has delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the Collector at 501-303-5620 for a payoff amount, and plan for the balance to be paid from the sale proceeds.
